name: Omar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run campaigns for Stridewell, a mid-sized running-shoe brand, and I'm the lead on our road-running line. My day is a stand-up at nine, then briefs, then a lot of back and forth with the design studio and the retail team about launch dates. I write a fair bit of the copy myself, the shoe-box inserts, the email headlines, the race-day posters. The long part is reporting, pulling numbers out of three dashboards every Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in any of that at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. If I'm stuck on email subject lines I'll ask a chatbot for twenty and steal the shape of one. I don't trust it with the brand voice yet. Money-wise, I'm on less than people get at the big sports brands, I'm still paying off my student loan, and my partner Lina and I have maybe three weeks of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Part of me thinks that's roughly what's happening already, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, that the tools are useful for grunt work and not much else. At the pub with my running club I'd joke that the robots still can't write a decent race-day poster. Online I'd probably not say anything, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for my job, but it doesn't fix my money. Stridewell's had two flat years and they froze pay rises in March. If AI only saves a bit of time, the saving goes to the shareholders, not to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot for subject lines and the Friday report, maybe save myself two hours a week. I'd ask for the pay rise again in my January review, with the numbers from the spring launch. And I'd keep paying off the student loan faster, an extra forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat. The scary story goes away, but the everyday squeeze stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the saving goes to shareholders. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it up at the staff forum, which is the closest thing we have to a union. Stridewell has no union, and I've thought for a while we should. A plateau doesn't change that, it just makes it less urgent for people, which is annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the January pay rise doesn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I start looking, quietly, though there's only one other sports brand in this city. Lina would say stay put until something real comes up. She's usually right about that kind of thing.

say: I'd say the tools help with **grunt work** and not much else.
I'd joke at **running club** that robots still can't write a race-day poster.
think: My job is fine, but **pay rises** stay frozen after two flat years.
Any time AI saves goes to **shareholders**, not to me.
do: Use the chatbot for **subject lines** and the Friday report.
Ask for the **pay rise** again in January with launch numbers.
Pay an extra **forty a month** off the student loan.
feel: Mostly fine, but **flat**, because the everyday squeeze stays.
S0.quote: The scary story goes away, but the everyday squeeze stays.
fieldNote: He sees this picture as **roughly today**, not a relief.
His frustration is about **who keeps** the time AI saves.
He wants a **union** but admits calm times make people lazy about it.

steps.text: Keep running the road-running campaigns at Stridewell
Use the chatbot to draft subject lines and the Friday report
Pay an extra forty a month off his student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the one I'd bet on. It's already creeping in at Stridewell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should lead on it, set rules for how we use it and keep people on the team. I'd say the brand voice needs a human owner. With my mates I'd be more blunt: firms will use this to hire fewer people and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my role survives but changes a lot, and the team around me shrinks. We've got six in marketing. I could see that becoming three plus software, and I'd probably be one of the three because I'm the lead. But that's my friend Jamie's job gone, and maybe the junior roles that I came up through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course on the AI tools, the paid one my manager mentioned, about four hundred, and ask Stridewell to cover it. I'd push to write the team's rules on how AI is used, so I'm the one shaping it. I'd also start talking to people about a union, because if cuts come, a staff forum won't stop them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot in my stomach about the others. I'd feel guilty for being one of the ones kept, if that's how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably be one of the three. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A marketing team of six could become three plus software, and I'm maybe sixty percent sure I'd be one of the three. Being the lead helps, but leads cost more, and someone younger who uses AI every day might look like a better deal. I'm not as quick with the tools as I'd need to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you were the one cut, what would you and Lina do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina's teaching salary covers the rent but not much else, so we'd cut the car first. I'd probably look at comms jobs at the council or a charity. With three weeks of savings, I'd take whatever came, honestly.

say: I'd say Stridewell should **set rules** for AI and keep people on the team.
With friends I'd say firms will **hire fewer** people and call it progress.
think: A team of six could become **three plus software**.
I'm maybe **sixty percent** sure I'd be one of the three kept.
do: Take the **paid AI course**, about four hundred, and ask work to cover it.
Push to **write the rules** on how the team uses AI.
Start talking to colleagues about forming a **union**.
feel: A **knot** in my stomach for the others.
**Guilt** at the thought of being kept while friends go.
S1.quote: A marketing team of six could become three plus software, and I'm maybe sixty percent sure I'd be one of the three.
fieldNote: He is **realistic** about odds and gives a number unprompted.
His progressive views show up as **guilt** about colleagues, not only fear.
He would **learn the tools** and organise at the same time.

steps.text: Take the paid AI marketing course and ask Stridewell to pay
Draft the team's written rules for using AI
Sound out colleagues about forming a union
Sell the car if he loses the job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's my whole job, basically. Everything I do is on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer right now, not a marketing one. Tax the firms selling it, pay people while they find their feet. I'd post that, which I never do, and I'd go on marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out within a year of it arriving. There's nothing in my day a robot needs hands for, so I don't get the three-year gap that hands-on jobs get. Lina's job has a person in a classroom, so hers probably lasts longer, but we can't live on one salary for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop the extra loan payments and put everything into savings, maybe a hundred and fifty a month. I'd look hard at jobs that need hands and people, like coaching. I'm a qualified run leader at the club, so I'd try to get paid coaching hours on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've been standing on a conveyor belt that suddenly sped up. Scared, and a bit numb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would coaching actually pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on its own. Maybe a couple of hundred a month to start. But it's something AI can't do while robots are still years off, and it's people standing in a park at seven in the morning. Running coaching is the one part of my life that needs my legs, not my laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your running club about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them half of us in that club work on screens, so we're all in the same boat. Maybe we'd organise something, a local group pushing the council for retraining money. People listen more when it's a group with a name.

say: I'd say this needs a **political answer** now, not a marketing one.
I'd post and **march** for taxing AI firms to pay people while they adjust.
think: Everything I do is on a screen, so I'm **out within a year**.
My partner's **teaching job** likely lasts longer, but one salary won't stretch.
do: Stop extra loan payments and save **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Get **paid coaching hours** at weekends as a qualified run leader.
Help the running club push the **council** for retraining money.
feel: **Scared** and a bit numb, like a conveyor belt that sped up.
S2.quote: Running coaching is the one part of my life that needs my legs, not my laptop.
fieldNote: He clearly sees that **screen work** gets no three-year grace period.
His fallback is a **hobby skill**, and he knows it won't pay enough.
He thinks in **groups**: the club, the council, the march.

steps.text: Stop extra student-loan payments and save a hundred and fifty a month
Start paid weekend coaching as a qualified run leader
Organise club members to lobby the council for retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to do something, if I start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them. At work I'd push Stridewell to commit to retraining staff instead of just cutting. Online I'd share stuff about unions and fair transitions, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see my marketing job as ending around 2031. The question is what I'm doing by then. Five years is long enough to get a coaching qualification and build a client list, I think, and the robots that could do that come later still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd do the level-two running coach course, about six hundred, and start coaching two evenings a week. I'd keep my Stridewell job and get as good as I can with the AI tools, because the better I am, the longer they keep me. And I'd save the coaching money, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less trapped. Like I've been given a map, but it's a long walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said get good with the AI tools to stay longer. Doesn't that speed things up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. It's a weird position, teaching the thing that replaces you. But if I don't, someone else will, and they'll be the one who stays. I'd rather be paid while I build the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Lina change, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been talking about buying a flat in a couple of years. I'd put that off. I wouldn't sign a mortgage on a job with a five-year clock on it.

say: I'd say we have a **few years**, so use them.
I'd push Stridewell to commit to **retraining staff** instead of cutting.
think: My marketing job likely **ends around 2031**, since it is all screen work.
Five years is enough to build a **coaching client list** before robots arrive.
do: Take the **level-two coach** course, about six hundred, and coach two evenings.
Get as good as I can with **AI tools** to stay employed longer.
feel: Anxious but **less trapped**, like holding a map for a long walk.
S3.quote: I wouldn't sign a mortgage on a job with a five-year clock on it.
fieldNote: Five years turns his **hobby** into a real plan.
He admits the **awkwardness** of training the tool that replaces him.
He would **delay buying** a home with his partner.

steps.text: Take the level-two running coach course, about six hundred
Get skilled with Stridewell's AI tools to stay on longer
Coach paid sessions two evenings a week and bank the money
Put off buying a flat with his partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven, which is still young, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a proper plan, so governments have no excuse. At work I'd say let's be the brand that treats its staff well through this. I'd probably say it with a bit more confidence than I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my marketing career probably has a decade, so I'd ride it out for a few years and build the coaching side slowly. My worry is less about me and more that by 2036 everyone will be trying to become a running coach. I'd want to be well in before the crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and use the AI tools more, since I'd have time to get properly good. I'd do the coaching course within two years, not straight away. And I'd still want that union at Stridewell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a slower worry, more like planning for a long winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone might try coaching. What's your edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being early and being local. If I've got ten years of club members who know me by 2036, that's worth more than a certificate. People pick coaches they've run next to in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the flat come back on the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a smaller one. Lina would want it, and with ten years we'd have a while to pay it down. But I'd want my coaching income steady first.

say: I'd say ten years leaves governments **no excuse**.
I'd want Stridewell to be the brand that **treats staff well**.
think: My marketing career likely has a **decade** left.
By 2036 the **crowd** will also try coaching, so I need to be early.
do: Keep the job and get **properly good** with AI tools.
Do the **coaching course** within two years.
Keep pushing for a **union** at Stridewell.
feel: Uneasy but **steady**, like planning for a long winter.
S4.quote: People pick coaches they've run next to in the rain.
fieldNote: More time makes him think about **competition**, not just survival.
His public **confidence** is a little ahead of how he feels.
Housing plans return, but only once **coaching income** is steady.

steps.text: Keep his Stridewell job and master the AI tools
Finish a running coach qualification within two years
Keep organising colleagues toward a union
Keep leading the road-running campaigns for now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no runway. What would help is a proper income floor while people retrain, and grants for courses like coaching that put people back with other people. And a law that says firms have to talk to staff before they swap them for software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about friends. I keep thinking about Jamie and the juniors more than myself. I've got a skill to fall back on, sort of; a lot of people my age just have a laptop and a login.

headlineQuote: A lot of people my age just have a laptop and a login.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** campaign lead at a running-shoe brand, using AI now and then.
He lives with his partner, a teacher, with about **three weeks** of savings.
He wants a **union** at work and blames shareholders for keeping AI's gains.
His fallback is **running coaching**, a hands-on skill robots reach years later.
With more warning he builds that plan early and **delays buying** a flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he would have no runway at all.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor** during retraining and grants for people-facing courses.
A law making firms **consult staff** before replacing them with software.
